tossups.text: In this country, a festival in which people throw tomatoes at each other takes place annually in Buñol. A town in this country uses a giant ball to chase people in an animal-friendly variant of the "running of the bulls" that originated in its city of Pamplona. Paella is often consumed at festivals in this country, where toreadors practice its native style of bullfighting. For 10 points, name this country, home to Valencia and Madrid.

This story's final line notes an "open space" between what a man "knew" and "tried to believe" that "nothing could be done about." A man in this story pins a postcard to a blood-stained shirt in honor of a character he thinks was killed with a tire iron. After discussing leaving for Mexico, a man in this story says "I wish I knew how to quit you." In this story, Alma Beers divorces her husband after noticing that he doesn't use his pole on fishing trips. As teenagers, this story's protagonists work for Joe Aguirre at the title location, where they take turns cooking meals and herding sheep. Larry McMurty won an Academy Award for co-writing a film adaptation of this story, which is collected in 1999's Close Range: Wyoming Stories. For 10 points, name this story by Annie Proulx about Jack Twist and Ennis del Mar's homosexual love affair, which was adapted into an Ang Lee film.

Minor characters in this work include the servant Christophil and a character who tries to frame a nobleman for murder, the deceitful Viluppo. One character has his servant kill Serberine because he believes that he informed the protagonist of his crime. Pedringano believes that a messenger is bringing him a pardon for murder, which prevents him from exposing Lorenzo. The protagonist's wife Isabella serves as a foil to Bel-Imperia, who loved Andrea before Balthazar killed him. For 10 points, name this revenge play centering on Hieronimo's attempt to avenge the death of his son Horatio, the most famous work of Thomas Kyd.

This man resigned from his position with the Treasury during the Versailles Conference and spent the following summer writing a book criticizing the Treaty of Versailles. This author of The Economic Consequences of the Peace wrote another book that explained price fluctuations in equity markets through the idea of his namesake "beauty contest," and this economist also argued that aggregate demand outweighed aggregate supply in terms of total economic impact. For 10 points, name this British economist known for his General Theory.

A practitioner of this social science began his career on Baffin Island studying migration patterns of Eskimos. One work in this field studied Japan and put forward ideas of "guilt" and "shame" societies, that book is The Chrysanthemum and the Sword by Ruth Benedict. Many early pioneers of their field studied at Columbia with Franz Boaz, who developed the concept of cultural relativism. For 10 points, name this social science, which is the study of mankind and its cultures.

A Carrolyn Frank work asks "Who Governed" this place, while Frederic van Holthoon analyzed the disenchantment it inspired in those who observed it. It was envisioned as a follow-up to a project about Elk Basin, and the work that bears its name includes the sections "The Long Arm of the Job" and "Making a Home." A sequel to that work discusses the Ball family's use of Mason Jars and is titled this place "in Transition," a reference to the Great Depression. The original, subtitled "A Study in Contemporary American Culture" was published in 1929. For 10 points, Muncie, Indiana was the basis for what place, the subject of two studies by Helen and Robert Lynd?

This character is "the Shaker God incarnated" according to a man who believes himself to be the archangel Gabriel. This character becomes a prophecy's first hearse during three chapters titled "The Chase." This is the main character discussed during a novel's nine "gams," or meetings. As a reward for the first person to see this character, a man offers a gold doubloon that he nails to a mast. Before accidentally killing himself, that man tells this character "From Hell's heart, I stab at thee!" The protagonist uses Queequeg's coffin as a lifeboat after this character destroys the Pequod. For 10 points, name this giant whale pursued by Captain Ahab in a novel by Herman Melville.

One ruler of this empire decapitated the "braggart" Teumman, king of Elam, and razed his capital of Hamanu, claiming in his chronicles that they had "plotted evil". That ruler also lost Egypt after Psamtik, with the help of Gyges of Lydia, rebelled. There were several phases of this empire, including one which climaxed during the rule of Tukulti-Ninurta I and another which reached the Mediterranean under Tiglath-Pileser I. Esarhaddon and Sennacherib, who conquered King Hezekiah, were other rulers of this empire. It was destroyed by the Medes and Chaldeans after the death of Asshurbanipal, and its major cities included Ninevah and Asshur. For 10 points, name this Mesopotamian empire centered north of Babylon.

Menestheus became king of Athens after slandering this figure, while for a time this figure was trapped in the underworld along with his friend Pirithous. This figure had originally traveled to the underworld to capture Persephone for his friend after they had kidnapped Helen, and on another famous journey, he defeated Cercyon in wrestling, stretched Sinis between his two trees, and placed Procrustes in his own torturous bed. This is, for 10 points, what hero who slew the Minotaur and caused his father's death by raising a black sail?

Before the premiere, tenor Raffaele Mirate ("mee-RAH-tay") was banned from humming an infectious canzone from this opera whose melody uses the following rhythm: "three accented eighths, then dotted sixteenth, descending thirty-second, quarter." In "Caro Nome" ("KA-ro NO-may"), the soprano lead of this opera praises her lover's fake name of "Gaultier Malde" ("go-tee-AY mald"). Francesco Piave's libretto for this opera, which adapts Le roi s'amuse ("luh RWAH sah-myooz"), was considered plagiaristic by the play's author Victor Hugo. This opera's title character remembers Count Monterone's curse when he opens a sack to find his dying daughter Gilda; that happens after he hears the Duke of Mantua reprise "La donna è mobile." For 10 points, name this Giuseppe Verdi opera titled for a hunchbacked jester.

In a work, this man claimed that "man would rather will nothingness than not will" and compared different types of morality with birds of prey and a lamb. This thinker stated that humans required amor fati, or a "love of fate," to accept the idea of eternal recurrence. This man criticized Kantian ethics and Christian morality as "slave morality" in a work because they are also based off of a good-evil dichotomy. Thus Spake Zarathustra and The Gay Science were written by, for 10 points, what German philosopher who famously proclaimed that "God is dead"?

An angel in this work etches the letter "P" into the narrator's head, and in another section, those who die bravely for Christianity are sent to Mars. Beginning with the line, "Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita", this work sees Caselia play music as others enter and another scene shows a character grind Ruggeiri's head. The narrator of this work meets Count Ugolino and Montefeltro, and describes the fate of Francesca. Seeing an icy area named Cocytus, this work includes the line, "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here." The narrator is guided through Heaven by his love Beatrice and led through Purgatory and Hell by Vergil in, for 10 points, what epic by Dante Alighieri?

Philip Anderson proposed a model named for this quantity that utilizes a triangular lattice and is one potential model for high temperature superconductivity. In one phenomenon present in Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids, this property is separated from charge, creating three independent quasiparticles. Operators projecting this property in the x, y and z directions can be found by multiplying h-bar over 2 by the corresponding Pauli matrix. Particles are separated based on this property in Stern-Gerlach experiments. An eponymous theorem uses relativity to differentiate between fermionic and bosonic statistics based on this property. For 10 points, name this intrinsic form of angular momentum that for fermions like the electron, is half-integer.

this structure is essential for antigen presentation. It plays a key role in the immune system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this T cell-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The T cell is a key component of the Immune system, involved in antigen presentation.

tossups.text: This civilization built roads called sacbeob, one of which connects its largest city to the Sacred Cenote. This civilization's Cocom dynasty was founded by Hunac Ceel, who ruled from his capital at Mayapam. The Temple of the Cross was built by this civilization in its city of Palenque. A mysterious leader named Spearthrower Owl conquered territory from this civilization for Teotihuacan [tay-OH-tee-hui-CAN], including its city of Tikal. This civilization used a shell to represent zero in its base-20 numeral system. For 10 points, name this civilization based in the Yucatan Peninsula, including the city of Chichen Itza.

This author asserted that Undine Spragg would be "a Page Six legend" in her introduction to a new edition of Edith Wharton's Custom of the Country. Riffing on James Wood, an LRB article by Lauren Oyler attacked this author's work as "hysterical criticism." In one essay, this author noted how it can feel like "solidarity is a matter of identity rather than politics or morality" to criticize hashtag activism. This onetime member of the "Repentagon" megachurch called scamming "the quintessential American ethos" in an essay on Trump's election included in a 2019 collection. That essay collection by this onetime star of the reality TV show Boys vs. Girls includes an essay partially about Sweetgreen titled "Always Be Optimizing." For 10 points, name this New Yorker columnist who wrote about internet culture in her best-selling book Trick Mirror.

The total synthesis of this compound is the subject of a 1963 Harvey Lecture that infamously dedicates a large amount of prose to eulogizing an intermediate retron. That total synthesis of this compound by Woodward heaps praise upon an isothiazole ring that smoothly allowed the synthesis of this compound's tropolonoid C ring. The biosynthesis of this molecule involves the coupling of the rings of autumnaline and the expansion of a tyrosine-derived ring to produce its two seven-membered rings. This compound reduces the frequency of attacks of familial mediterranean fever. This compound was the first to be found to arrest mitosis by binding to tubulin, thus preventing tubulin's polymerization. For 10 points, name this therapeutic compound extracted from the autumn crocus that is used to treat acute gout flares.

This man wrote Discord Among the Enemy and The Edge of the Sword, and he argued for mechanized warfare and the building of tanks in The Army of the Future. This man was president during student rioting in May 1968. This man became president of his country after a rebellion in Algeria, and was succeeded by Georges Pompidou. For 10 points, name this leader of the Free French during World War II, who later founded the French Fifth Republic.

A man with this regnal name was the first king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth but only reigned for about a year. Another king with this name signed the Treaty of Cateau-Cambresis shortly before he was killed in a jousting accident. An event known as the Day of the Barricades occurred during a war fought between three men with this name. Francois Ravaillac [rah-vah-YAK] assassinated the last French king of this name, who quipped "Paris is well worth a mass." For 10 points, identify this name shared by some French kings, the fourth of whom was born in Navarre and gave religious liberty to the Huguenots by issuing the Edict of Nantes.

The Netherlands fought for independence from this country during the Eighty Years War. During the reign of Philip II, poor winds foiled this country's attempted invasion of England using a namesake "Armada" of ships. This country was unified by the marriage of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. For 10 points, name this country on the Iberian Peninsula whose capital is Madrid.

parts.text: Name this country, whose city of Vladivostok lies near its border with North Korea. It is the largest country by area.
Kamchatka and Vladivostok are located in this cold, eastern region of Russia. This region is crossed by a namesake railway, and stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean.
A valley named for these features in the Kamchatka Peninsula contains two hundred examples of them. The name of these geological features draws from one located in the Haukadalur valley of Iceland.

bonuses.leadin: The Sea of Okhotsk ["o-KOHT-sk"] is west of this country's Kamchatka ["kahm-chaht-kah"] Peninsula. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this story in which Eber decides not to commit suicide after he witnesses a boy fall into an icy pond. This story titles a 2013 collection.
Tenth of December is a collection by this author of the collections CivilWarLand in Bad Decline and Pastoralia.
Saunders won a Booker Prize for his novel titled for this historical figure "in the Bardo," which begins with a party hosted by this president's wife, Mary Todd.

bonuses.leadin: This story begins with a character pretending to save his crush Suzanne Bledsoe from the Netherworlders. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this author of the story "Red Pyramid." Near the end of a novel by this author, men have sex in a "caterpillar" formation while shouting "Hail!"

In "Red Pyramid," Yura misses one of these events by taking a train to Fryazino instead of Fryazevo. In a Dostoevsky novella, Yakov Golyadkin meets his double after being kicked out of one of these events.
acceptableAnswers: prompt on dinner party by asking “for what sort of occasion?”

parts.text: In another Sorokin story, Burmistrov claims to have subsisted on only horse soup for seven years while in one of these places. In a novel, Kilgas the Latvian and the Baptist Alyoshka live in one of these places.

bonuses.leadin: In a short story by this author, a character yells whimsical expletives like "Shitomometer!" and "Foolodancius!" before meeting a man with a "large, mealy-white, pear-shaped face." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name these canines studied by Ivan Pavlov.
Pavlov taught dogs to drool at the sound of a bell, demonstrating the classical form of this phenomenon, which is contrasted with its operant form.

B. F. Skinner conditioned these animals to exhibit superstitious behavior, such as head-nodding while waiting for food. Skinner also operantly conditioned these birds to play ping pong and guide missiles.

bonuses.leadin: UPenn professor Martin Seligman electrocuted these animals to induce learned helplessness. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Stephen Rogata tried to scale this skyscraper, Trump's residence in New York City. During Cinco de Mayo, Donald Trump took a picture of himself eating a taco bowl at Trump Grill, a restaurant in this building.
Donald Trump criticized Gonzalo Curiel's rulings regarding this institution, which allegedly used misleading marketing methods. This now defunct institution did not offer degrees to its students.
Donald Trump owns 17 of these facilities, one of which he recently opened in Aberdeen, Scotland. One of these facilities in New Jersey will host the 2017 Women's Open.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, name these institutions owned by the Donald:

parts.text: Identify this quantity, which, when plotted against strike price, often displays a namesake "smile." This forward-looking value is derived from the prices of certain financial instruments.

Implied volatility can be figured out by looking at the prices of these contracts. The "call" variety of them gives the holder the right to buy the underlying at a certain price at some time in the future.
This formula, later improved by Robert Merton, prices options by assuming that the log returns are a random walk with constant volatility, in a constant interest-rate environment.

bonuses.leadin: This quantity can be found pretty quickly using Newton's method if you know the value of vega. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this poet who composed Requiem after the authorities detained her husband Nikolay Punin in 1938.
Akhmatova's requiem memorializes victims of the Great Purge of this Soviet leader. This leader was fictionalized as Number 1 in Arthur Koestler's Darkness at Noon.

Akhmatova used the line, "I have lit my treasured candle," to open a poem titled for the lack of one of these people. Joseph Campbell examined the monomyth in a book titled for [one of these people] with a Thousand Faces.
acceptableAnswers: accept The Hero with a Thousand Faces

bonuses.leadin: This poet bemoans "seventeen months I've pleaded for you to come home", in a poem about the imprisonment of her son. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this 1954 Supreme Court case which ruled against the doctrine of "separate but equal" and overturned Plessy v. Ferguson.
acceptableAnswers: Board of Education of Topeka v. Brown

parts.text: Three years after the Brown decision, this state's governor Orval Faubus attempted to use the National Guard to stop desegregation of Little Rock Central High School in this state's capital.

During the hearing of Briggs v. Elliott, a case later combined with Brown, two psychologists with this surname named Kenneth and Mamie used their "doll experiment" to testify on the self-esteem issues produced in black children by segregation.

bonuses.leadin: This case built on a decision involving the University of Texas Law School, Sweatt v. Painter. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Identify this warrior, who fought an entire army in single combat during the Cattle Raid of Cooley. He was taught by Scathach, who gave him the spear Gae Bulg, and gained his name from slaying a guard dog in his youth.
The Cattle Raid of Cooley was instigated by this Queen of Connaught, who was often referred to with the epithet "of the friendly thighs." She died via projectile cheese.
Cu Chulainn and Queen Medb are figures from this country's Ulster Cycle, whose folklore also includes tales of banshees and leprechauns.

bonuses.leadin: This hero's father was either Sualtam mac Roich or the god Lugh, depending on the source. For 10 points each:

parts.text: In addition to staff notation, Guido created a note-labelling system based on syllables in the hymn Ut queant laxis. That system was the precursor to this one, where the "ut" was replaced by an open syllable.
The medieval composers Leonin and Perotin were innovative in their use of polyphony in plainchant. The two were part of the Notre Dame school, which was based in this city of France.
An early medieval composer was this abbess, known as the "Sybil of the Rhine." She composed many liturgical songs and wrote Ordo Virtutum, the oldest known morality play.

bonuses.leadin: In the early 11th century, Guido d'Arezzo became an influential figure in the development of music notation and education. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This first of the Pauline epistles is also the longest. Its eighth chapter champions those who live "by the spirit" over those who live "by the flesh".

Immediately succeeding Romans is this letter, whose 13th chapter, often read at weddings, states that of "faith, hope and love, the greatest of these is love." It also contains Paul's statement that we see "through a glass, darkly".
This epistle is directed to a Roman province in Anatolia. Preceding Ephesians, it focuses on the controversy of the Gentile Christians and urges believers to "not be desirous of vain glory."

bonuses.leadin: 1. For 10 points each, name these Pauline epistles:

parts.text: Identify this short story in which the Misfit and his accomplices murder Grandma and her family after a car accident.
parts.answer: Good Man is Hard to Find
acceptableAnswers: Good Man is Hard to Find
The Good Man is Hard to Find

parts.text: This American author wrote "A Good Man is Hard to Find" and included short stories like "Greenleaf" and "A View of the Woods" in her collection, Everything that Rises Must Converge.

This character in the short story "A Good Man is Hard to Find" is the only character to say the title phrase. He is the owner of the Tower restaurant and converses with Grandmother about the Misfit during her lunch break.

bonuses.leadin: In this work, the cat Pitty Sing leaps on Bailey, causing him to flip his car. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Operators in quantum mechanics are all Hermitian, which means their eigenvectors form a basis according to this theorem which states normal matrices can be diagonalised by unitary transforms.
Any two operators A and B share a basis of eigenvectors if and only if this function on them is zero, in which case the associated quantities can be measured simultaneously in quantum mechanics.
The commutator of two operators also appears in this principle named for Heisenberg, which is normally stated in terms of position and momentum.

bonuses.leadin: Many basic properties of quantum mechanics are related to theorems of linear algebra. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name the primary structure associated with villi and microvilli.
What is the main function of the duodenum in the digestive system?
Name another component of the digestive system related to villi and microvilli.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, answer these questions about the human digestive system.

parts.text: Sumer was located in the "Fertile Crescent" between the Tigris River and this river. This longest West Asian river begins in Turkey and empties into the Persian Gulf.
This Akkadian conqueror of Sumer is said to have founded the world's first empire. This king's daughter Enheduanna is the first recorded poet in history.
Before its ultimate collapse, Sumer experienced a renaissance during the Third Dynasty of this city, which saw the writing of the Epic of Gilgamesh. This city was home to the Great Ziggurat.

bonuses.leadin: For ten points each, answer these questions about Mesopotamia's earliest civilization, Sumer:

parts.text: Among the literature of these people were a namesake collection of historic "chronicles" and poems that used literary devices called kennings. They were notably ruled by Harold Godwinson and Invaded England with the Jutes.
This most famous of the Anglo-Saxon poets is this man, author of a poem beginning "Now we must praise heaven-kingdom's Guardian," his "Hymn."
The only proof of the existence of this poet is four poems with epigraphs containing his name in the Exeter and Vercelli books. His poem Elene is an account of St. Helena finding the true cross.

parts.text: In statics, these structures consist of two-force members so that they behave overall as single objects. They typically consist of straight members, which only experience pure tension or compression, connected at joints.
When analyzing a truss, one typically assumes it is in this configuration - that is, all the forces and torques at each joint sum to zero.

Forces inside a truss can be calculated by the method of joints, the method of sections, or this graphical method. It involves creating "force polygons" by drawing the vectors at each joint in the proper size and scale.

bonuses.leadin: Name some things about statics, for 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this strongman from Roman myth who wore the skin of the Nemean Lion.
The Tower of Hercules is this type of building that helps approaching ships navigate toward safe harbor oraway from dangerous coastlines.

Another navigational aid on the west end of the Mediterranean Sea is a pair of mountains that this ancientRoman historian named the "Pillars of Hercules." This historian died while trying to rescue a friend during theeruption of Mount Vesuvius.

bonuses.leadin: A navigational aid on the coast of Galicia in northwest Spain, dating from the first century CE, is namedafter this mythical man because it marks the western limit of his travels. For ten points each,

parts.text: Name this environmental disaster in the Midwest that occurred about the same time as the Great Depression, which caused the mass migration of thousands of "Okies."
This president, who initiated the New Deal, attempted to stop the Dust Bowl with the Great Plains Shelterbelt, which planted over 200 million of trees in the Midwest.
A New Deal-sponsored documentary about the Dust Bowl was titled [this thing] That Broke the Plains. One factually-incorrect saying about the Midwest stated that rain followed this object.
acceptableAnswers: The Plow That Broke the Plains

bonuses.leadin: One cause of this event decreased crop yields in Russia due to the Russian Revolution, which led to overcultivation of crops in the United States. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This 1862 act gave about 160 acres of land to those who lived on and improved the land for five years.
This 1887 act allowed the U.S. government to survey Indian tribal lands and divide them up among the individuals in the tribe to assimilate Indians into American society.
In 1889, the Indian Territory - land that is now this state - was opened to settlement and a Land Rush followed. This state's Sooners arrived early to the land.
